name: Sigma
license: DRL 1.1 (rules); LGPL 2.1 (pySigma, sigma-cli); specification public domain
summary: An open YAML format for detection rules over log events, with a community repository of more than 3,000 rules and tools that convert them into each SIEM’s query language.
intro: A Sigma rule describes suspicious log events in YAML. `logsource` says which logs it applies to in generic terms, such as `product: aws` with `service: cloudtrail`, or `category: process_creation` on Windows, rather than naming an index or a product. `detection` holds named selections: a map of fields that must all match (AND) or a list of alternatives (OR), with modifiers such as `contains`, `endswith` or `re` after a pipe. `condition` combines the selections with `and`, `or`, `not` and patterns like `1 of selection_*`. Metadata such as `level`, `status`, `falsepositives` and MITRE ATT&CK `tags` travels with the rule. The project’s README puts it this way: “Sigma is for log files what Snort is for network traffic and YARA is for files.”

Since specification 2.0 (August 2024), correlation rules sit on top. A correlation references other rules by `id` or `name`, groups their matches by fields such as `User`, and fires on a count of events (`event_count`), a number of distinct values (`value_count`) or a set or sequence of rules (`temporal`, `temporal_ordered`) within a `timespan` such as `10m`. Version 2.1 (August 2025) added sums, averages and percentiles of a field.

Sigma itself runs nothing. pySigma, a Python library, parses rules and converts them through backends into a target’s query language: Splunk SPL, Elasticsearch Lucene or EQL, Kusto (KQL) for Microsoft Sentinel and Defender XDR, and more than 30 others on the Sigma backends page. Processing pipelines map Sigma’s field names and log sources onto the target’s schema, such as the Elastic Common Schema. The `sigma` command (sigma-cli) wraps pySigma, and engines such as RSigma evaluate rules directly against events.
strengths: Write once, run on many SIEMs: the same rule converts to Splunk, Elasticsearch, Sentinel, QRadar, CrowdStrike and more than 30 backends in all
A large free rule set: more than 3,000 peer-reviewed rules in the SigmaHQ repository (generic, threat hunting, emerging threats, compliance), released as packages every quarter
Plain YAML files suit detection as code: they live in Git, get reviewed in pull requests and deploy through CI/CD
Built into other tools: MISP, VirusTotal, Security Onion and IBM QRadar, among others, support Sigma rules natively
limits: No engine of its own: results depend on the backend, type modifiers such as `re` work only where the backend supports them, and pySigma and sigma-cli still carry a pre-release status badge
Field mapping is the hard part: rules use Sigma’s generic field names, so every data source needs a pipeline that maps them to the names in your logs
Deliberately limited: basic searches plus a few correlation types, chosen to cover most day-to-day needs; anything beyond needs the target’s own query language
Licenses differ by part: the rules’ Detection Rule License 1.1 requires keeping the rule’s author attribution when you share rules and in alert messages based on their matches

sections.title: The parts of Sigma
sections.intro: “Sigma” names a format, a rule collection and a toolchain, each in its own repository and under its own license.

items.name: Specification
items.text: The rule, correlation and filter formats, with appendices for modifiers, tags and the taxonomy of field names and log sources, plus JSON schemas. Version 2.1.0 was released on August 2, 2025.

items.name: Rule repository
items.text: SigmaHQ/sigma: more than 3,000 rules in folders for generic detections, threat hunting, emerging threats, compliance and placeholder rules, published as rule packages on the releases page.

items.name: pySigma
items.text: The Python library that parses rules and converts them. Backends for query languages and pipelines for log data models ship as separate packages, to keep the core slim and vendor-agnostic.

items.name: sigma-cli
items.text: The `sigma` command on top of pySigma: `sigma plugin install splunk`, then `sigma convert -t splunk -p sysmon rules/`. It replaced the legacy `sigmac`, which reached end of life on August 1, 2024.

sections.title: Converting rules with sigma-cli
sections.intro: A backend picks the query language and pipelines map the fields; the same rules can feed several targets.
source: # process-creation rules into Splunk queries for Sysmon logs
# the same rules as a Splunk savedsearches.conf file
sigma convert -t splunk -f savedsearches -p sysmon -o savedsearches.conf sigma/rules/windows/process_creation

story: Analysts shared indicators of compromise and YARA rules for malicious files, but had no common way to describe a detection in log events, so searches built for one SIEM stayed there. Florian Roth came to Thomas Patzke with an already concrete idea for a signature format for log events. They refined it by trading voice messages, and the next day Roth wrote the first rules: the commit “First Example Set”, with rules for a cleared event log and for failed logon reasons, is dated December 24, 2016.

Over two to three months they worked through problems such as different field naming conventions, solving them in the rule language and the converter, much of which Patzke wrote. Sigma was released in 2017, and Patzke presented it at Hack.lu that year. Both had built it out of their own pain handling incidents, and large organizations often run several SIEMs: with Sigma, a rule written once could become a Splunk or ArcSight query, an Elasticsearch query or a grep one-liner. MISP added native Sigma support in March 2017, and by 2019 some users listed Sigma support as a requirement when buying security products.

The original converter, `sigmac`, was replaced by pySigma, a library with backends and pipelines in separate packages, and its command-line front end sigma-cli. Specification 2.0 in August 2024 dropped the old aggregation expressions for correlation rules and added filters, and `sigmac` reached end of life on August 1, 2024. The project now lives in the SigmaHQ organization, maintained by a group that includes Roth and Patzke along with Nasreddine Bencherchali, Christian Burkard, François Hubaut and others.

choices.why: The Sigma FAQ says YAML is easy to read and write, flexible and has all the language elements needed, while admitting it lacks a standardized schema language like XML’s (the specification later added JSON schemas).

choices.choice: Generic log sources instead of product-specific ones
choices.why: One rule with `category: process_creation` replaces separate rules for Sysmon, Windows Security auditing and kernel process events; converters map the abstract log source to the right indexes, so the rule isn’t tied to one telemetry source.

choices.choice: Convert to each SIEM rather than ship an engine
choices.why: Organizations already ran Splunk, ArcSight and Elasticsearch side by side. Converting meant writing a rule once for all of them; Patzke said they would be fine with the converter becoming obsolete through native Sigma support, as YARA and Snort have in many products.

choices.choice: Simple searches and a few common correlations
choices.why: The design covers basic searches and counts, which the project says meet more than 90% of day-to-day detection needs, in exchange for rules that can be shared across all sorts of security environments.

timeline.text: Florian Roth commits the first example rules on December 24
Sigma is released; MISP 2.4.70 adds native support in March; Thomas Patzke presents it at Hack.lu
`sigmac` reaches end of life on August 1; specification 2.0 adds correlation rules and filters on August 8
Specification 2.1 adds sum, average and percentile correlations on August 2
Quarterly rule packages continue, the latest released in July
